cards.front: Define the contrapositive of a conditional statement, and say why it matters.
cards.back: The contrapositive of $P \Rightarrow Q$ is $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$. It always has the same truth value as the original, so proving it proves the original.

keyPoints.text: negate both parts and reverse them
proving the contrapositive is a legitimate proof of the original
synonyms: it is a valid proof strategy

mcq.correct: $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$, always equivalent to $P \Rightarrow Q$
distractors: $Q \Rightarrow P$, always equivalent to $P \Rightarrow Q$
$\neg P \Rightarrow \neg Q$, always equivalent to $P \Rightarrow Q$
$\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$, equivalent only when $P$ is true

cards.explanation: Because the equivalence is unconditional, the contrapositive is a genuine alternative route to a proof and is often the easier one: 'if $3n + 2$ is odd then $n$ is odd' is awkward forwards but immediate as 'if $n$ is even then $3n + 2$ is even'.

cards.front: Define the converse and the inverse of $P \Rightarrow Q$, and say which pairs are equivalent.
cards.back: The converse is $Q \Rightarrow P$ and the inverse is $\neg P \Rightarrow \neg Q$. These two are equivalent to each other, and neither is equivalent to the original.

keyPoints.text: converse and inverse are equivalent to each other
neither is equivalent to the original
synonyms: the original pairs with the contrapositive

mcq.correct: Converse and inverse are equivalent to each other; neither matches the original
distractors: All four forms are equivalent
Converse and contrapositive are equivalent
Inverse and original are equivalent

cards.explanation:
The four forms split into two equivalence classes: $\{P \Rightarrow Q,\ 
eg Q \Rightarrow 
eg P\}$ and $\{Q \Rightarrow P,\ 
eg P \Rightarrow 
eg Q\}$. Taking the contrapositive of the inverse gives the converse, which is why the second pair travels together. Confusing the classes is the fallacy of affirming the consequent.

cards.front: What does 'A is necessary for B' mean as an implication, and how does it differ from 'A is sufficient for B'?
cards.back: 'A is necessary for B' means $B \Rightarrow A$: B cannot hold without A. 'A is sufficient for B' means $A \Rightarrow B$: A alone guarantees B. A condition may be one, both or neither.

synonyms: a condition can be one, both or neither

mcq.correct: Necessary: $B \Rightarrow A$. Sufficient: $A \Rightarrow B$
distractors: Necessary: $A \Rightarrow B$. Sufficient: $B \Rightarrow A$
Both mean $A \Rightarrow B$; the words are interchangeable
Both mean $A \Leftrightarrow B$

cards.explanation: The reliable reading is that 'if' attaches to the sufficient condition and 'only if' to the necessary one: 'you can graduate if you pass' is $P \Rightarrow G$, while 'you can graduate only if you pass' is $G \Rightarrow P$. When both hold, $A \Leftrightarrow B$, and the condition is necessary and sufficient.

cards.front: What is a vacuously true statement?
cards.back: A conditional whose hypothesis is never satisfied. Since $P \Rightarrow Q$ is false only when $P$ holds and $Q$ fails, such a statement cannot fail and is therefore true.

synonyms: no case can make it fail

mcq.correct: A conditional with an impossible hypothesis, which is true by default
distractors: A statement that is neither true nor false
A statement true only for some values
A statement that has not yet been proved

cards.explanation: 'If $n$ is an even prime greater than 2, then $n^2 = 7$' is vacuously true, since no such $n$ exists. Vacuous truth also explains why 'every element of the empty set has property P' is true for any P at all, which surprises candidates the first time they meet it.

cards.front: What is the difference between inclusive and exclusive 'or' in mathematics?
cards.back: Mathematical 'or' is inclusive: '$A$ or $B$' holds when at least one of them holds, including when both do. Exclusive 'or' would exclude the case where both hold.

synonyms: at least one of the two

keyPoints.text: the case where both hold is allowed
exclusive or would exclude that case

mcq.correct: Inclusive: true when both hold
distractors: Exclusive: false when both hold
Depends on the topic being discussed
Undefined until the statements are made precise

cards.explanation: Consequence: the solution set of '$x > 0$ or $x^2 > 4$' is the union of the two sets, and since $x > 2$ is already inside $x > 0$ the answer collapses to $x > 0$ or $x < -2$. Reading 'or' as exclusive, or as 'and', is a routine source of lost marks.

cards.front: State De Morgan's laws for the negation of a conjunction and a disjunction.
cards.back:
$
eg(P \wedge Q) = 
eg P \vee 
eg Q$ and $
eg(P \vee Q) = 
eg P \wedge 
eg Q$: negation turns 'and' into 'or' and 'or' into 'and'.

keyPoints.text: not (P and Q) is (not P) or (not Q)
not (P or Q) is (not P) and (not Q)
the connective flips as the negation passes through
synonyms: De Morgan swaps and and or

acceptedAliases: not(P and Q) = not P or not Q; not(P or Q) = not P and not Q

mcq.correct:
$
eg(P \wedge Q) = 
eg P \vee 
eg Q$ and $
eg(P \vee Q) = 
eg P \wedge 
eg Q$
distractors:
$
eg(P \wedge Q) = 
eg P \wedge 
eg Q$

$
eg(P \vee Q) = 
eg P \vee 
eg Q$
$\neg(P \wedge Q) = P \vee Q$

cards.explanation:
The laws also cover quantifiers, which is where they earn their keep on Paper 2: $
eg( orall x\, P) = \exists x\, 
eg P$ and $
eg(\exists x\, P) =  orall x\, 
eg P$. Pushing a negation through a quantifier flips it, exactly as pushing one through 'and' turns it into 'or'.

cards.front: What does it mean that the order of quantifiers matters? Give an example.
cards.back: 'For every $x$ there is a $y$ such that $P(x, y)$' and 'there is a $y$ such that for every $x$, $P(x, y)$' are different claims. The second is stronger: one single $y$ must work for all $x$.

keyPoints.text: the two orders are not equivalent
synonyms: swapping the quantifiers changes the meaning
one y must serve every x
for every x there is y with x + y = 0 but no single y works for all x

mcq.correct: They are different claims; the version with $\exists y$ first is stronger
distractors: They are equivalent because both quantify over the same variables
The order matters only when the statements are false
Order matters only for uncountable sets

cards.explanation: With $P(x, y)$ being $x + y = 0$: for every $x$ there is a $y$, namely $-x$, but no single $y$ satisfies it for every $x$. Reversing the quantifiers turns a true statement into a false one. When negating, flip each quantifier but keep the order: $\neg(\forall x\,\exists y\, P) = \exists x\,\forall y\, \neg P$.

cards.front: What is a counterexample, and what can and cannot it establish?
cards.back: A single case that fails a universal claim. One counterexample disproves 'for all $x$, $P(x)$', but no number of successful examples proves it.

keyPoints.text: one case is enough to disprove a for-all statement
examples cannot prove a universal claim
synonyms: finitely many checks are not a proof

mcq.correct: Disproves a universal claim with one case; cannot prove one
distractors: Proves a universal claim if enough of them are found
Disproves an existential claim with one case
Proves an existential claim only when combined with a general argument

cards.explanation: The asymmetry is worth memorising: universality is cheap to refute and expensive to prove, existence is cheap to prove and expensive to refute. So disproving 'there exists $x$ with $P(x)$' needs a general argument that $P$ fails everywhere.

cards.front: Name the fallacy in this argument: 'If it rains the ground is wet. The ground is wet. Therefore it rained.'
cards.back: Affirming the consequent: from $P \Rightarrow Q$ and $Q$ it concludes $P$, which is the converse and does not follow.

synonyms: the ground could be wet another way

mcq.correct: Affirming the consequent
distractors: Denying the antecedent
Circular reasoning
Begging the question

cards.explanation:
The valid forms are modus ponens ($P \Rightarrow Q$, $P$, so $Q$) and modus tollens ($P \Rightarrow Q$, $
eg Q$, so $
eg P$). Affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent ($P \Rightarrow Q$, $
eg P$, so $
eg Q$) are the two invalid mirrors, and both show up as distractors in Paper 2 argument questions.

cards.front: What is the fallacy of denying the antecedent?
cards.back: From $P \Rightarrow Q$ and $\neg P$ it concludes $\neg Q$. It is invalid: the implication says nothing about what happens when $P$ fails.

keyPoints.text: it concludes not Q from not P
synonyms: the inverse is treated as if it were equivalent
if it rains the ground is wet; it did not rain, so the ground is not wet

mcq.correct: From $P \Rightarrow Q$ and $\neg P$ concluding $\neg Q$
distractors: From $P \Rightarrow Q$ and $Q$ concluding $P$
From $P \Rightarrow Q$ and $\neg Q$ concluding $\neg P$
Concluding $P$ and $Q$ are equivalent without proof

cards.explanation: The third option, modus tollens, is valid - which is what makes the two easy to confuse. Denying the antecedent amounts to assuming the inverse $\neg P \Rightarrow \neg Q$, and the inverse is equivalent to the converse, not to the original.

cards.front: What are the two parts of a proof by induction, and why are both indispensable?
cards.back: The base case, verifying the statement at the first value, and the inductive step, showing that if it holds for $k$ then it holds for $k + 1$. Without the base case there is nothing to start the chain; without the step the chain does not propagate.

synonyms: assume for k and prove for k + 1

mcq.correct: Base case and inductive step; either alone proves nothing
distractors: Base case and a worked example; the step follows
Inductive step only; the base case is a formality
Three cases, $n$, $n + 1$ and $n + 2$

cards.explanation: A correct inductive step with a false base case still 'proves' false statements, which is why exam questions ask candidates to find the missing base case. Both parts together give: the statement holds at the start, and truth propagates one step at a time, so it holds throughout.

cards.front: What is proof by exhaustion, and when is it the right choice?
cards.back: Checking every case in turn, which is valid only when the cases are finite and can be listed completely. It suits claims about a small finite set, such as the divisors of a number or residues modulo a small integer.

keyPoints.text: only valid when the cases are finite and complete

mcq.correct: Check all finitely many cases, valid only when the list is complete
distractors: Check enough cases to make the result convincing
Argue from a representative example
Assume the result and derive a contradiction

cards.explanation: Exhaustion is a real proof method, unlike checking a few examples, precisely because nothing is left out. It becomes the method of choice in the disguise of proof by cases on residues: to prove 'if $n^2$ is divisible by 3 then $n$ is divisible by 3', exhaust $n = 3k, 3k + 1, 3k + 2$.

cards.front: What does 'without loss of generality' mean, and what must be true for it to be justified?
cards.back: That the cases not written down reduce to the one being treated, usually by symmetry. It is justified only when the remaining cases genuinely follow the same argument, not merely because they look similar.

keyPoints.text: the other cases reduce to this one
synonyms: the omitted cases behave the same way

keyPoints.text: it must be justified, not asserted

mcq.correct: The omitted cases reduce to the one treated, usually by symmetry
distractors: The result can be assumed for the omitted cases
The proof is incomplete but acceptable
The author has checked the other cases numerically

cards.explanation: Used properly it is a genuine saving: proving $a + b = b + a$ for non-negative reals and saying the other sign combinations follow by symmetry is fine, because negation is a symmetry of the reals. Used as a substitute for an argument it is exactly the gap a Paper 2 'find the flaw' question is built around.

cards.front: Define the discriminant of a quadratic and state what each of its signs tells you about the roots.
cards.back: The discriminant of $ax^2 + bx + c$ is $b^2 - 4ac$. Positive gives two distinct real roots, zero gives one repeated real root, and negative gives no real roots.

mcq.correct: $b^2 - 4ac$: two, one repeated, none
distractors: $b^2 + 4ac$: two, one repeated, none
$b^2 - 4ac$: one, two, none
$4ac - b^2$: two, one repeated, none

cards.explanation: Zero still counts as real roots, which is why 'has real roots' needs $b^2 - 4ac \ge 0$ while 'has two distinct real roots' needs the strict inequality. Geometrically the discriminant records how many times the parabola meets the $x$-axis, and it drives every 'find the range of $k$' question on Paper 1.

cards.front: What is frequency density on a histogram, and how is frequency recovered from it?
cards.back: Frequency density is frequency divided by class width, plotted on the vertical axis. Frequency is therefore frequency density times class width, which is the area of the bar.

keyPoints.text: frequency = frequency density x class width
the modal class is the tallest bar, not the largest frequency

mcq.correct: Frequency divided by class width; frequency is the area of the bar
distractors: Frequency multiplied by class width; frequency is the height of the bar
The cumulative frequency; frequency is the gradient
Frequency per unit time; frequency is the total

cards.explanation: Because bars have unequal widths, only the area is comparable, so the modal class is the one with the greatest frequency density. Reading the tallest bar as having the largest frequency is the standard trap: a wide bar with modest density can hold more data than a narrow tall one.

cards.front: What is a surd, and what is meant by rationalising the denominator?
cards.back: A surd is an irrational root such as $\sqrt{2}$ left in exact form. Rationalising the denominator means rewriting a fraction so that no root appears in the denominator, usually by multiplying top and bottom by a conjugate.

keyPoints.text: remove the root from the denominator

mcq.correct: An exact irrational root; remove roots from the denominator using a conjugate
distractors: Any decimal approximation; round the denominator
A fractional index; rewrite as a power
A negative root; take the absolute value

cards.explanation: For $\frac{3}{\sqrt{7} - 2\sqrt{3}}$ multiply by $\frac{\sqrt{7} + 2\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{7} + 2\sqrt{3}}$; the denominator becomes a difference of two squares, $7 - 12 = -5$. The same conjugate trick handles nested radicals such as $\sqrt{12 + 6\sqrt{3}}$, by squaring $a + \sqrt{b}$ and matching rational against irrational parts.

cards.front: What is a stationary point, and how are the three types distinguished?
cards.back: A point where $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$. A sign change from positive to negative is a maximum, from negative to positive a minimum, and no sign change a stationary point of inflection.

keyPoints.text: + to - is a maximum, - to + is a minimum
no sign change is a point of inflection

mcq.correct: $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$, classified by the sign change either side
distractors: $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$, classified by the value of $y$
$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 0$ always
Any turning point or any point of inflection

cards.explanation: The second derivative test is a shortcut but fails when $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 0$, as it does for $x^4$ at 0, so the sign change of the first derivative is the reliable criterion. Stationary points are what make 'three distinct real roots' questions work: the maximum must sit above the axis and the minimum below it.

cards.front: What is an extraneous root, and which operations create one?
cards.back: A value produced by an algebraic step that does not satisfy the original equation. Squaring both sides and multiplying by an expression that can be zero are the two operations that create them.

keyPoints.text: a root of the manipulated equation that fails the original
synonyms: it does not satisfy the original equation

keyPoints.text: multiplying by something that may be zero

mcq.correct: A solution of the manipulated equation that fails the original; created by squaring
distractors: A solution found by a numerical method
A root that cannot be written exactly
A complex root of a real equation

cards.explanation: Solving $\sqrt{2x + 3} = x$ by squaring yields $x = 3$ and $x = -1$, but $x = -1$ gives $\sqrt{1} = -1$, which is false. The remedy is to substitute every candidate back, or to state the domain restriction - here $x \ge 0$ - before starting.

cards.front: What is the difference between a lemma, a corollary and a conjecture?
cards.back: A lemma is a subsidiary result proved on the way to a larger one, a corollary is a result that follows immediately from one already proved, and a conjecture is a statement believed true but not yet proved.

keyPoints.text: lemma: a stepping stone to a bigger result
corollary: follows immediately from a proved result

mcq.correct: Lemma is a stepping stone, corollary an immediate consequence, conjecture unproved
distractors: Lemma and corollary are unproved, conjecture is proved
All three are synonyms for a theorem
Conjecture means disproved

cards.explanation: The distinction matters when reading an argument: a conjecture carries no logical weight at all, however convincing the evidence, and $n^2 + n + 41$ being prime is the classic example of a conjecture that survives 39 cases and then fails. A corollary, by contrast, is already proved once the result it follows from is.

cards.front: What is a telescoping series, and what is the general method for summing one?
cards.back: One whose terms cancel in a regular pattern when written out. Split the general term into partial fractions, write out the first few and last few terms, and add up only what survives.

keyPoints.text: terms cancel in a regular pattern

mcq.correct: Terms cancel; split into partial fractions and add what survives
distractors: Terms grow without bound; compare with a geometric series
Terms alternate in sign; group them in pairs
Terms repeat periodically; sum one period

cards.explanation: $\sum \frac{1}{n(n+2)}$ splits as $\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{n+2}\right)$, and because the gap is 2 rather than 1 two terms survive at each end, giving $\frac{1}{2}(1 + \frac{1}{2}) = \frac{3}{4}$. Counting how many terms survive is the step most often got wrong: the gap in the denominators is exactly that number.

cards.front: State the alternate segment theorem.
cards.back: The angle between a tangent and a chord through the point of contact equals the angle subtended by that chord in the alternate segment.

keyPoints.text: angle between the tangent and the chord
equals the angle in the alternate segment
synonyms: equals the angle the chord subtends on the far side

keyPoints.text: equal to the angle at the circumference standing on the same chord

mcq.correct: The tangent-chord angle equals the angle in the alternate segment
distractors: The tangent-chord angle equals the angle at the centre
The tangent-chord angle is always a right angle
The tangent-chord angle equals the angle between the chord and the diameter

cards.explanation: If the chord $AB$ subtends $130^\circ$ at the centre, then a point $C$ on the major arc gives angle $ACB = 65^\circ$, and the angle between the tangent at $A$ and $AB$ is also $65^\circ$. This was a reported emphasis in the October 2024 sitting, usually inside a multi-step angle chase rather than as a one-line recall.

cards.front: What does 'if and only if' mean, and what must a proof of such a statement contain?
cards.back: It means the two statements are equivalent: $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ is both $P \Rightarrow Q$ and $Q \Rightarrow P$. A proof must establish both directions separately.

synonyms: P implies Q and Q implies P

keyPoints.text: neither direction follows from the other
proving one direction leaves the proof incomplete

acceptedAliases: P <=> Q means P implies Q and Q implies P

mcq.correct: Both $P \Rightarrow Q$ and $Q \Rightarrow P$ must be proved
distractors: Proving $P \Rightarrow Q$ is enough
Proving either direction is enough
It means the statements have the same truth value in one example

cards.explanation: '$n$ is even if and only if $n^2$ is even' needs both halves. The forwards direction is one line; the backwards direction is genuinely harder and is usually done by contrapositive, since $n$ odd gives $n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1$ odd. Delivering only the easy half is one of the standard ways Paper 2 questions award partial credit and no more.
